extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, students of poetics, and literary critics studying classical dramatic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing tragic (and epic) poetry focused on unity of action, proper ordering (beginning/middle/end), just magnitude, temporal extent, verisimilitude, and selection of episodes so the whole forms one coherent imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beginning / Middle / End must be properly ordered
rubrics_metrics.description: The Beginning is followed by something and is necessarily preceded by something; the Middle precedes the End; nothing ought to follow the End.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beginnings, Middles and Ends are distinct parts that must stand in the proper order. Do not give 'a Beginning to the Beginning' or add material after the rightful End (example: adding present effects after Achilles's end is a fault attributed to Statius).

rubrics_metrics.name: Middle parts must presuppose and require context
rubrics_metrics.description: The Middle is that which supposes something which ought to precede it, and requires something which ought to follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Middle should not itself have a beginning or end independent of the principal action; it must have respect to the beginning of the principal action (be its effect) and terminate in the end of which it is a cause. Middles that are entire by themselves and do not depend on the main action are foreign to the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid foreign, self-contained episodes (epicodes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Middle parts or episodes that are entire by themselves (suppose nothing before them and require nothing after them) are not parts of an action and are foreign to the subject of the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such foreign episodes break the unity of the Theban action (example: Statius's episode about Hypsipyla). They make something complete and independent from the rest and should be rejected as unrelated to the principal action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not arbitrarily begin or end the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet must not make his Beginning when something ought necessarily to precede it, nor give an End when something must necessarily follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beginnings and Ends must flow from necessity or probability in the action's economy; inventing a beginning or an end that ignores necessary antecedents or consequents distorts the action and is a fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Just and reasonable magnitude (proper extent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever is fine and composed of parts must not only be in order but must have a just and reasonable magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A subject should be neither too small nor too large for its kind: if too small it is weak; if too large it confuses order and prevents a coherent apprehension. The measure is when the whole can be perceived or retained by the audience (compare to bodily beauty and magnanimity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceptible apprehension: sight and memory limits
rubrics_metrics.description: For visible objects the eye must be able to run over the parts in an insensible moment; similarly, the memory must be able to receive and retain all the parts of a dramatic subject without trouble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A subject too small is seen all at once and loses interest; a subject too large cannot be grasped and is confusing. Choose an extent such that spectators can apprehend and remember the whole (example: Sophocles' Oedipus is arranged so memory can retain it).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration of representation should match the action's necessary/probable time
rubrics_metrics.description: The duration of the representation should neither be fixed by arbitrary rules nor be longer/shorter than the action it imitates; it depends on the nature of the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While no universal fixed rule applies, the representation should occupy roughly the time required by the action's plausibility. When impossible, poets may compress by probability/verisimilitude but must avoid violating likelihood. Use messenger reports or intervals to cover longer real-time events, provided probability and measure are preserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use verisimilitude to compress time, but preserve probability
rubrics_metrics.description: If the real action would take longer than is possible to represent, the poet may shorten it by recourse to verisimilitude (probability), not by violating credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compress incidents so that the audience believes they could have happened in the represented time. Crowding too many real incidents into a short representation destroys probability and beauty (examples: attempts to compress 24–30 hours into a few hours are risky).

rubrics_metrics.name: A larger extent may improve a piece only to a limit
rubrics_metrics.description: The larger the extent any piece has, the finer it will be, provided it is not so large that the subject cannot be comprehended at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increase extent only until the subject can still be apprehended as a coherent whole; beyond that, enlarging the piece diminishes clarity and beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: A dramatic/epic imitation must represent one unified action
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the fable is an imitation of an Action, that Action must be one and entire; its different parts must be so linked that transposing or removing any sensibly alters or destroys the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid composing a poem from all the adventures of a hero (e.g., all Achilles's actions); select those incidents that together form a single, coherent, necessary or probable sequence (Homer and Virgil exemplify this unity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Essentiality test: parts whose omission causes no sensible change are not part of the action
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever can be put in, or left out, without causing a sensible change cannot be a part of an action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a test to distinguish true epicodes from false ones; if an episode adds nothing to or subtracts nothing from the principal action when omitted, it is a foreign or superfluous member (example: the episode of Hypomnes in Statius's Thebaid).

rubrics_metrics.name: Epicodes must be necessary or probable consequences of the main action
rubrics_metrics.description: Epicodic fables or episodes used by poets ought to be connected so that one is a necessary or probable consequence of another and of the principal action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include only episodes that have a ground in the fable and are joined to the principal action as natural causes or effects (example: Ulysses' wound causing later remembrance is an appropriate episode; feigned madness has no necessary relation and is rightly omitted by Homer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Epicodes should be imperfect, dependent members not complete actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Good epicodes are imperfect members which, taken alone, finish nothing; they contribute to and depend on the principal action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An episode that constitutes a complete, independent action does not belong as an episode in tragedy or epic because it breaks unity (contrast proper epicodes in Homer with independent episodes in lesser poets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet must follow truth or verisimilitude rather than mere factual history
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet does not relate things exactly as they happened but as they might or ought to happen — he treats universal (what must or probably will happen), while the historian treats particular what did happen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry is more 'solid and moral' because it treats general truths; poets may invent names and particulars provided the actions are credible and exemplify universal character or moral truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using fictional or real names: credibility decides usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic poets often use true names, but may impose invented names; what matters is that the events are credible and possible — true past events make credibility easier but are not necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy typically invents names freely; tragedy may use true names but can invent when it better serves probability and universality (example: Agathon's Flower uses invented names and still pleases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise (peripeteia/anagnorisis) is necessary to tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Surprise is necessary to tragedy (heading indicates the importance of producing surprise in the fable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The fable should be constructed so that dramatic reversals or recognitions arise naturally from necessity/probability, producing a surprising but credible effect for the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and study are required even for great natural genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Even the greatest natural genius needs to be polished, enriched and strengthened by study of rules; neglecting rules leads to faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Corneille wrote inferior pieces before learning dramatic rules; Statius likely lacked acquaintance with the Art of Poetry and thus committed errors. Study rules to avoid common faults despite natural talent.
